floors.title: first floor
floors.intro: नमस्ते! Read the नमस्ते label in this room to learn how to play.

tutorial.text: Read the text in the panel below and press OK.
Tap the pulsing target to walk there.
Tap the door द्व to walk through it.
Tap the label नामकरणम्, read how naming works and press OK.
Now the rabbit शशः: tap it, then tap it again to walk beside it and read its name.

entities.m: vowel signs, in the order of the vowels
entities.info: The vowel signs, each placed where its vowel stands in the room of vowels.

entities.m: bridge: decipher each stone to step on it
entities.info: Two paths of stepping stones made of look-alike letters. Decipher a stone to raise it.

A temple with people and gods from the word list. Two places by the fire wait for the crown मुकुटम् and the jewel रत्नम् from the far shores of the water room: walk onto each place with the object in your स्यूतः. When both are placed, the great door on the right opens.
The fourteen vowels in their traditional order. Stand beside each one to learn it.
The first row of consonants, the ka-varga: ka kha ga gha ṅa.

entities.m: vowel signs on ka, kha, ga, gha, ṅa
entities.info: Each consonant of the ka row with every vowel sign. The door needs क and ग from your bag.
The door below (द्वारम्) opens when the crow काकः is here with you. It flies around in a room in the far west, past the rooms of the ca row and the ṭa row. Name it, and it will follow you back here.

Namaste! You are अ, short for अहम् aham = “I”. This is Akṣaraloka, a world written in Devanagari. Tap the floor to walk. Go beside a word or letter and tap it to learn to read it: unknown words are written in black and get their colours once you can read them. Letters can be picked up into your स्यूतः bag, and some doors need them. Animals and fire block the way until you name them. What you learn fades over time, so come back and read it again. Labels like this one tell you more. Start through the door on the right.

Animals live in this world. They are not fought: an animal blocks your way until you name it. Stand beside it, tap it and read its name. Some animals ask you to build their name or to know what it means.
वाक् vāc is the power of speech. Here sounds and words are magic: reading a word gives it its colour, naming a creature calms it, and the letters you collect open doors.

Everything in this world is written: animals, objects, fire, doors and people all appear as their Sanskrit word, so to know a thing you read its word. Naming: stand beside a creature and tap it. Its name appears split into its akṣaras; choose the right sound for each part, one after the other. A wrong choice costs nothing but the word’s level, so at the beginning just try: trial and error is a good way to start. Once named, the creature calms down and lets you pass.

Every consonant carries a short a: क is ka, not just k. The short a is the most common sound in Sanskrit, so the script does not write it: it is built into every consonant. A vowel sign replaces it (कि ki, कु ku), and the virāma ् removes it (क् k). Learn the vowel अ and the consonant क here.
The second row of consonants, the ca-varga: च ca, छ cha, ज ja, झ jha, ञ ña. They are spoken with the tongue against the palate. Like every consonant, each carries a short a.

The door below (द्व) leads to the consonants. It opens with the vowels अ a and आ ā from this room and the vowel sign ◌ा ā from the room of vowel signs to the east. Pick them up into your स्यूतः: stand beside each, learn it, then press Pick up. Short a has no vowel sign, because every consonant already carries it.
The third row of consonants, the ṭa-varga or cerebrals: ट ṭa, ठ ṭha, ड ḍa, ढ ḍha, ण ṇa. The tongue curls back to the roof of the mouth; in transliteration they carry a dot below.
A crow flies around in this room. Name it and it will follow you. Bring it to the room of the ka row: there it opens the door down to the vowel signs on consonants.

deliver.name: the room of the ka row (व्यञ्जनानि)

entities.info: Signs that change a syllable without being a vowel: ◌ं anusvāra adds a nasal after the vowel (कं kaṃ), ◌ः visarga adds a breath (कः kaḥ), ◌ँ candrabindu makes the vowel nasal (कँ kam̐), and ◌् virāma removes the inherent a (क् k).
The fourth row of consonants, the ta-varga or dentals: त ta, थ tha, द da, ध dha, न na. The tongue touches the upper teeth. Compare them with the ṭa row above: there the tongue curls back.
The fifth row of consonants, the pa-varga or labials: प pa, फ pha, ब ba, भ bha, म ma. They are made with the lips.
The semivowels य ya, र ra, ल la, व va stand between vowels and consonants: they sound close to i, ṛ, ḷ and u.
The sibilants and the breath: श śa (palatal, like sh), ष ṣa (retroflex, tongue curled back), स sa (dental) and ह ha. They are made with a stream of air.

When two consonants meet with no vowel between them, they are written together as one ligature: the first one loses its inherent a. Usually you can still see both parts (स्त sta, न्त nta, द्य dya); र below a consonant becomes a small stroke (प्र pra, त्र tra, श्र śra); and some ligatures have a shape of their own: क्ष kṣa and ज्ञ jña. The stairs lead down to harder ligatures.

entities.info: The inner sanctum of the temple, opened by the crown and the jewel. Here sits शिवः.

Śiva, “the auspicious one”, one of the great gods. He destroys what has grown old so that something new can begin, and he is the lord of yoga and of dance (naṭarājaḥ). His name ends in the visarga ◌ः like most masculine words you have met: शिवः śivaḥ. Above his sanctum lies the last room.
A hermitage of sages and teachers. The horse at the gate has to be named before you can enter.

entities.m: what is here is also elsewhere
entities.info: Mahābhārata 1.56.34. First half of the saying. Its single words joined by sandhi: yat iha → yad iha · iha asti → ihāsti · tat anyatra → tad anyatra.

entities.m: what is not here is nowhere
entities.info: Mahābhārata 1.56.34. Second half of the saying. Its single words joined by sandhi: yat na → yan na · na iha → neha · neha asti → nehāsti · tat kvacit stays tat kvacit.

The last room. A saying from the Mahābhārata lies here in its single words, in reading order from left to right and top to bottom. Read each word and pick it up. When all twelve are in your स्यूतः, they join into the saying above, and the door at the top opens.

इति iti, “thus”: the word that closes a text in Sanskrit. You walked through the world of letters and read your first verse. Come back now and then: what you learned fades, and the world will bring it back to you.
A tree in the crow’s room.
The gateway to level 2: the system of Sanskrit sounds.

floors.title: संयुक्तानि — ligatures
floors.intro: You climb down into the hall of ligatures. Each room shows one family of joined letters.

entities.info: Welcome to the hall of harder ligatures. Each room shows one family. Read the parts from top to bottom and from left to right; the first consonant always loses its a. The stairs lead back up.
ह joins the next consonant in its own way: ह्म hma and ह्न hna put the second sign under ह, ह्य hya and ह्व hva join to the right, ह्र hra hangs the ra stroke below.
द stacks the next consonant below it: द्ध ddha, द्व dva, द्म dma, द्भ dbha, द्ग dga. Look for the small sign hanging under द.
A nasal joins the consonant of its own row: ङ्क ṅka, ङ्ग ṅga (ka row), ञ्च ñca, ञ्ज ñja (ca row), ण्ड ṇḍa (ṭa row), न्द nda (ta row), म्ब mba (pa row). Often the anusvāra ◌ं is written instead.
A tiger prowls through this room. If it runs into you before you have named it, it throws you back to the stairs. Stand beside it and build its name to calm it.

र changes most: before a consonant it rides on top as a hook (र्क rka, र्म rma, र्य rya, the repha); after a consonant it is a small slanted stroke (क्र kra, ट्र ṭra); and with u or ū it takes special shapes (रु ru, रू rū). कृ kṛ uses the vowel sign ṛ.
Three consonants can join, too: स्त्र stra, न्त्र ntra, ष्ट्र ṣṭra, क्ष्म kṣma, त्त्व ttva. Read them part by part: स्त्र is s + t + ra.

floors.title: स्थानानि — places of sound
floors.intro: You step through the gateway into the second level: the sounds of Sanskrit and where in the mouth they are made.

entities.info: Level 2 follows chapter 2 of Ruppel’s Cambridge Introduction to Sanskrit: the system of Sanskrit sounds. The order of the letters follows three principles: from simple to complex (first the vowels, which can be spoken on their own, then the consonants), from the back to the front of the mouth, and similar sounds grouped together. The five chambers above the hall are the five places of articulation, from the back of the mouth to the lips. Go down into the hall.

The throat. Velars: the air is briefly stopped at the back of the throat, at the velum. The vowels a ā are spoken low at the back of the mouth, and h belongs here too (do not confuse h with visarga ḥ). The stops k kh g gh ṅ and their nasal belong here. Bring these five letters from the hall and walk onto their places.
It burns low. When all five letters of this place are on their pedestals, it blazes up.
A lamp of the hall. It shines up when the five letters of the chamber above are in their places.

The palate. Palatals: the tongue touches the hard palate. With them go the vowels i ī, their glide y and the palatal sibilant ś. The stops c ch j jh ñ and their nasal belong here. Bring these five letters from the hall and walk onto their places.
It burns low. When all five letters of this place are on their pedestals, it blazes up.
A lamp of the hall. It shines up when the five letters of the chamber above are in their places.

The roof of the mouth. Retroflexes: the tongue is curled back (“retroflected”) to touch the roof of the mouth. With them go the vowels ṛ ṝ, their glide r and the retroflex sibilant ṣ. The stops ṭ ṭh ḍ ḍh ṇ and their nasal belong here. Bring these five letters from the hall and walk onto their places.

entities.info: It burns low. When all five letters of this place are on their pedestals, it blazes up.
A lamp of the hall. It shines up when the five letters of the chamber above are in their places.

The teeth. Dentals: the tongue touches the teeth (Latin dent- “tooth”). With them go the vowel ḷ, its glide l and the dental sibilant s. The stops t th d dh n and their nasal belong here. Bring these five letters from the hall and walk onto their places.
It burns low. When all five letters of this place are on their pedestals, it blazes up.
A lamp of the hall. It shines up when the five letters of the chamber above are in their places.

The the two lips. Labials: the lower and upper lips touch (Latin labia “lips”). With them go the vowels u ū, which are spoken with rounded lips, and their glide v. The stops p ph b bh m and their nasal belong here. Bring these five letters from the hall and walk onto their places.
It burns low. When all five letters of this place are on their pedestals, it blazes up.
A lamp of the hall. It shines up when the five letters of the chamber above are in their places.

The hall of sounds. The twenty-five letters of the five rows lie here, mixed up. Read and pick up each one, and bring it to the chamber of the place where it is spoken. When all twenty-five are in place, the door at the bottom right opens.

The simple vowels are a ā i ī u ū ṛ ṝ ḷ, each short then long. Then come the complex vowels e ai o au. At an earlier stage of the language they were the diphthongs *ai *āi *au *āu, so the pattern short – long continues here, and all four count as long. The nasal of each row (ṅ ñ ṇ n m) is spoken at the place of its stops, with the way into the nose open.

floors.title: प्रयत्नः — voice and breath
floors.intro: The second floor of level 2: how a sound is spoken, with or without voice and breath, and which syllables are heavy.

entities.info: Each row of five has the same order, from simple to complex: unvoiced unaspirated (k), unvoiced aspirated (kh), voiced unaspirated (g), voiced aspirated (gh), nasal (ṅ). Stops in the same row share their place; stops in the same column share their manner. Voiced: put a finger on your throat and say d, then t; with d you feel the vocal cords vibrate. Aspirated: hold your hand before your mouth and say pot, then spot; the puff of air in pot is aspiration. kh, th, ph … are one sound each, and th is never the English th of thanks.
A ripe fruit. Someone on this floor would like it.

entities.info: The river of voice. Voiced sounds make the vocal cords vibrate: g gh j jh ḍ ḍh d dh b bh, the nasals ṅ ñ ṇ n m, the glides y r l v and h (h is voiced in Sanskrit, though today it is mostly spoken unvoiced). Unvoiced are k kh c ch ṭ ṭh t th p ph and the sibilants ś ṣ s. Only voiced stones carry you: read a stone, and if it is unvoiced, it sinks.

entities.why: भ bha is a light syllable (laghu) — it sinks

क ka is a light syllable (laghu) — it sinks
श śa is a light syllable (laghu) — it sinks

entities.info: Chapter 2A: heavy and light syllables. A syllable is heavy when it contains a long or complex vowel (ā ī ū ṝ e ai o au), when its vowel is followed by more than one consonant (so it ends in a consonant itself, like kun), or when its vowel is followed by anusvāra ṃ or visarga ḥ. It is light when it has a short vowel (a i u ṛ ḷ) followed by at most one consonant. A single consonant between vowels starts the next syllable: bha-ra-ti. Only heavy syllables carry you: read a stone, and if it is light, it sinks.

Śa-kun-ta-lā: kun is heavy because it ends in a consonant, lā because its vowel is long. Word stress: if the second-last syllable is heavy, it is stressed; if it is light, the stress goes back to the third-last. ta is light, so the stress falls on kun: Śakúntalā. Likewise bha-rā-mi has the stress on rā, and in bha-ra-ti, all light, it goes back to bha.
A parrot sits in the doorway and does not move. Naming it is not enough: it moves only for a fruit, फलम्. Then it flies around in its room.

Why the order of sounds matters: from the root √bhaj “to allot; to honour, worship” come bhāj- “worshipping”, bhāga- “portion” and bhakti- “worship”. A palatal (j) appears as its velar counterpart (g), and a voiced sound (g) as its voiceless counterpart (k) before another voiceless sound. Knowing these relations means you understand words instead of memorising each one.

The end of level 2. You now know the order of the Sanskrit alphabet: by place, from throat to lips, and by manner, unvoiced or voiced, with little or much breath, and nasal. And you can tell heavy from light syllables.
